reasoning: Both sets are strong, detailed plans built with the same toolchain. A is closer to what the user actually asked for. Its spec requires every world and variant to beat both random and rule-based play (paired permutation test with Holm correction, plus every run above the rule baseline), and it adds explicit write-up support for the 'explain why it works' goal. Its roadmap splits the fish tank by real dependency (one fish → many fish → local sight). M1 is a true walking skeleton: an online Q-learning spine that M2 thickens into full DQN. Its contract freezes only M1's boundaries and defers the rest. A's weaknesses: S1 is split into M2 (tuned DQN + viewer) and M3 (reference check + write-up), which reads partly as carving to cut size. Some test items are stale (TC-07 direction 'to be re-derived', the TC-17 bound unresolved inside an M1 task). Some packets leave out types they need (core.Step and WorldSpec in T09, the check budget in T03, holm's signature in T25). B has richer RL teaching ladders (REINFORCE vs PPO, naive co-learning vs an opponent pool), very concrete hand-checkable golden cases (I checked TC-07, TC-12, TC-42 and TC-58) and more complete packets. But B's brief is stale ('Designing future environments now' is listed as Not doing, and success is stated only for Snake). B lowers the Snake bar to 'not worse than scripted' plus 'at least one agent beats scripted', and has no write-up support. Its contract freezes M2/M3 types and helper maths functions in the M1 interface, with a bloated RunSettings. And it has one huge milestone per stage, with no walking skeleton (the M1 DQN spine is the full DQN, size M). On balance A's plan fits the user better and is more proportionate.
